Jeroboam’s wife got up and went to Sarira. When she came to the doorway of the house, the child died.
All Israel mourned him and buried him, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the prophet.
The rest of Jeroboam’s deeds, how he fought and how he reigned, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Jeroboam reigned for twenty-two years. He rested with his fathers, and his son Nebat reigned in his place.

Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned over Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned for seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the Lord had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite.
Rehoboam did evil before the Lord. He emulated everything his fathers had done and followed the sins they had committed.
They built high places and sacred groves for themselves on every high hill and beneath every leafy tree.
There were also cult prostitutes in the land, and they practiced all the abominations of the nations that the Lord had driven out before the children of Israel.
In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.

He took all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king’s house, and the gold spears that David had taken from Hadadezer king of Zobah and brought to Jerusalem—all that he had taken. He also took the gold shields that Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place, and the commanders of the guards who guarded the doors of the king’s house took charge of them.
Whenever the king entered the house of the Lord, the guards would carry them and then set them down in the guards’ wing.
And the rest of Rehoboam’s deeds and everything he did—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.
Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite, and his son Abijah reigned in his place.
And in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijah son of Rehoboam became king over Judah.
He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah, daughter of Absalom.
And he followed the sins his father had committed before the Lord his God, and his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord his God, as the heart of his father David had been.
For David’s sake, the Lord God gave him a surviving line in Jerusalem, to establish his son after him and to make Jerusalem secure.
Just as David did what was right before the Lord and did not turn aside from anything he commanded him throughout his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam throughout his life.
The rest of Abijah’s deeds and everything he did—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.
Abijah rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place.
In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa became king over Judah.
He reigned for forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah, daughter of Absalom.
Asa did what was right before the Lord, like his father David.
He removed the cult prostitutes from the land and abolished all the corrupt practices his fathers had established.
He also removed his mother Maacah from her position as queen, because she held gatherings in her sacred grove. Asa demolished her strongholds and burned them with fire in the Kidron ravine.
However, he did not remove the high places. Nevertheless, his heart was wholly devoted to the Lord throughout his days.
He brought his father's pillars and brought his own pillars into the house of the Lord: silver, gold, and vessels.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their lives.
Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built up Ramah so that no one could go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.

Asa took all the silver and gold found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king's house, and entrusted it to his servants. King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad, son of Abenraim, son of Hazael, king of the Syrians, who lived in Damascus, saying:

“Make a covenant between me and you, and between my father and your father. Look, I have sent you a gift of silver and gold. Break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.”
Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent his commanders against the cities of Israel. He struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinnereth, as far as the whole land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard this, he stopped building up Ramah and returned to Tirzah.

King Asa commanded all Judah who were in Enakim to take away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had built. With them King Asa built up the entire hill of Benjamin and the watchtower.
The rest of Asa's deeds, all his might, everything he did, and the city he built—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age his feet became diseased.
Asa rested with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His son Jehoshaphat became king in his place.
Nadab son of Jeroboam became king over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel for two years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed his father's way and his sins, by which he caused Israel to sin.
Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, plotted against him. Baasha struck him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, while Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon.
Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and became king in his place.

When he became king, he struck down the whole house of Jeroboam. He left no living soul in the house of Jeroboam until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the Lord, which he had spoken through his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.
This was because of all the sins Jeroboam committed and caused Israel to commit, and because of the provocation with which he provoked the Lord, the God of Israel.
The rest of Nadab's deeds and everything he did—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
There was war between Asa and Nadab king of Israel throughout their lives.
And in the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned for twenty-four years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and his sins, by which he caused Israel to sin.
The word of the Lord came through Jehu son of Hanani to Baasha, saying:

“Because I raised you from the earth and made you ruler over my people Israel, but you followed the way of Jeroboam and caused my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their worthless idols,
look, I will rise up against Baasha and against his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city, the dogs will eat; and anyone belonging to him who dies in the fields, the birds of the sky will eat.”
The rest of Baasha's deeds, everything he did, and his might—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Baasha rested with his ancestors and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah became king in his place in the twentieth year of King Asa.

Through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani, the Lord spoke against Baasha and his house because of all the evil he had done in the Lord’s sight, provoking him to anger by the works of his hands, becoming like the house of Jeroboam, and because he had struck him down.
In the twenty-sixth year of the king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king over Israel in Tirzah for two years.
His servant Zimri, commander of half his armed forces, conspired against him. Elah was drinking and was drunk in the house of Arza, the keeper of the wardrobe, in Tirzah.
Zimri entered, struck him down, and killed him in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and became king in his place.
When he became king and sat on his throne, he struck down the entire house of Baasha. He left him not a single male, nor any of his relatives or friends.
Zimri wiped out the entire house of Baasha, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken against the house of Baasha through the prophet Jehu,
because of all the sins of Baasha and his son Elah, who sinned and made Israel sin, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols.
And the rest of Elah’s deeds and everything he did—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned for seven days in Tirzah. The army of Israel was at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines.
The people in the camp heard it said, “Zimri has conspired and struck down the king.” That day in the camp, the Israelites made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel.
Omri and all Israel with him went up from Gibbethon and besieged Tirzah.
And when Zimri saw that the city had been taken, he entered a chamber in the king’s house and burned the king’s house down over himself.
He died because of the sins he had committed, doing evil in the Lord’s sight and following the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the sins he had committed, by which he made Israel sin.
The rest of Zimri’s acts and the conspiracies he formed—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Then the people of Israel were divided. Half the people followed Tibni son of Ginath to make him king, and half the people followed Omri.
The people who followed Omri prevailed, and the people who followed Tibni son of Ginath were defeated. Tibni and his brother Joram died at that time, and Omri became king after Tibni.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri became king over Israel for twelve years. He reigned in Tirzah for six years.
Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer, the owner of the hill, for two talents of silver. He built up the hill and named the hill he had built up Samaria, after Shemer, the owner of the hill.
Omri did evil in the Lord’s sight and acted more wickedly than all who had come before him.
He followed all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and his sins, by which he made Israel sin, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols.
The rest of Omri’s acts, everything he did, and the mighty deeds he performed—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Omri rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab became king in his place.
Ahab son of Omri became king over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah. Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria for twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did more evil in the Lord’s sight than all who had come before him.
It was nothing to him to follow the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. He took as his wife Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and bowed down to him.
He erected an altar to Baal in the house of his abominations, which he built in Samaria.
And Ahab made a grove, and Ahab did more to provoke the Lord, the God of Israel, than all the kings of Israel who had been before him.

In his days Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho. At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundations, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he erected its gates, according to the word of the Lord, which he spoke through Joshua son of Nun.

Elijah the prophet, from Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, “As the Lord, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at the word of my mouth.”
The word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying:
“Go east from here and hide in the ravine of Cherith, which faces the Jordan.
You shall drink water from the ravine, and I will command the ravens to feed you there.”
And Elijah went and did according to the word of the Lord. He went and stayed in the ravine of Cherith, opposite the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank water from the ravine.
After some days the ravine dried up, because there had been no rain upon the earth.
The word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying:
“Rise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians and stay there. See, I have commanded a widow there to feed you.”
He rose and went to Zarephath, to the city gate. There was a woman gathering wood. Elijah called after her and said to her, “Bring me a little water in a vessel so that I may drink.”
She went to bring it, and Elijah called after her and said, “Bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.”

The woman said, “As the Lord your God lives, I have no loaf, only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. I am gathering two sticks, and I will go in and prepare it for myself and my children. We will eat it and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Take courage. Go in and do as you have said, but first make me a small loaf from it and bring it to me. Afterward make some for yourself and your children.
For this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour shall not run out, and the jug of oil shall not diminish until the day when the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth.’”
The woman went and did according to Elijah’s word, and she and he and her sons ate.
From that day onward, the jar of flour did not run out, and the jug of oil did not diminish, according to the word of the Lord, which he spoke through Elijah.
After these things, the son of the mistress of the house became ill. His illness was so severe that no breath remained in him.
She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, man of God? Have you come to me to bring my sins to remembrance and kill my son?”
Elijah said to the woman, “Give me your son.” He took him from her arms, carried him up to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him on his side on his own bed.
Elijah cried out and said, “Alas for me, Lord, you who are a witness for the widow with whom I am staying! You have afflicted her son by putting him to death.”
And he breathed on the child three times and called on the Lord, saying, “O Lord my God, let this child’s breath return to him.”
And so it happened: he cried out, and the Lord heard Elijah’s voice. The child’s breath returned into his body, and he came to life.
Elijah took the child, brought him down from the upper room into the house, and gave him to his mother. Elijah said, “See, your son is alive.”
The woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.”
After many days, the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying, “Go and present yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the face of the earth.”
Elijah went to present himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
Ahab called Obadiah, his commander of a thousand. Obadiah feared the Lord greatly.
When Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them in caves, fifty in each, and fed them with bread and water.

The king said to Obadiah, “Come, let us go through the land to all the springs of water and the streambeds. Perhaps we will find grass and keep the horses and mules alive, so that the livestock do not perish.”
They divided the route between them to travel through the land. Ahab went alone along one route, and Obadiah went alone along another.
While Obadiah was on the road, Elijah came alone to meet him. Obadiah hurried, fell on his face, and said, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
Elijah said, “It is I. Go and tell your master, ‘Elijah is here.’”
And Obadiah said, “What sin have I committed that you are handing your servant over to Ahab to kill me?”

“As the Lord your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my master has not sent to search for you. When they say, ‘He is nowhere here,’ he burns the kingdom and its land because he has not found you.
“And now you say, ‘Go and tell your master, “Elijah is here.”’

“When I leave you, the Spirit of the Lord will carry you away to a land I do not know. I will go in to tell Ahab, but he will not find you and will kill me. Yet your servant has feared the Lord from his youth.
“Was my lord not told what I did when Jezebel was slaughtering the Lord’s prophets? I hid a hundred men from among the Lord’s prophets, fifty men in each cave, and fed them with bread and water.”
“And now you say to me, ‘Go and tell your master, “Elijah is here.”’ He will kill me.”
And Elijah said, “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will appear before him today.”
Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him. Ahab hurried away to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to Elijah, “Is it you, the one who troubles Israel?”
Elijah said, “I do not trouble Israel, but you and your father’s house do, because you have abandoned the Lord your God and followed the Baals.

“Now send and gather all Israel to me on Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, the four hundred and fifty prophets of shame, and the four hundred prophets of the groves who eat at Jezebel’s table.”
Ahab sent throughout all Israel and gathered the prophets on Mount Carmel.
Elijah brought all the people near and said to them, “How long will you limp between two paths? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal is, follow him.” The people gave him no answer.
Elijah said to the people, “I alone remain as a prophet of the Lord, but the prophets of Baal number four hundred and fifty men, and the prophets of the grove four hundred.

“Let them give us two bulls. Let them choose one for themselves, cut it into pieces, and lay it on the wood, but put no fire under it. I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood, but I will apply no fire.
“You shall call on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of the Lord my God. The god who answers with fire is God.” All the people answered, “What you have said is good.”
Elijah said to the prophets of shame, “Choose a bull for yourselves and prepare it first, since you are many. Call on the name of your gods, but put no fire under it.”

They took the bull he gave them, prepared it, and called on the name of Baal from dawn until noon, saying, “Hear us, Baal! Hear us!” But there was no voice and no response. They ran around the altar they had made.

At noon Elijah the Tishbite mocked them and said, “Call out loudly, for he is a god! Perhaps he has something to amuse him, or perhaps he is issuing a command, or perhaps he is asleep and will wake up.”
They called out loudly and cut themselves with swords and spears according to their custom, until blood poured over them.

As evening drew near, they continued prophesying until the time for offering the sacrifice, but there was no voice. Elijah the Tishbite spoke to the prophets of the abominations and said, “Stand aside; now I will make my burnt offering.” They stood aside and went away.
Elijah said to the people, “Come near me.” All the people came near him, and he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been demolished.
Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, to whom the Lord had spoken, saying, “Your name shall be Israel.”
He built with the stones in the name of the Lord and made a trench around the altar large enough to hold two measures of seed.
He piled the wood on the altar he had made, cut up the burnt offering, and laid it on the wood, placing it on the altar.

He said, “Bring me four jars of water and pour them over the burnt offering and the wood.” Then he said, “Do it a second time,” and they did it a second time. He said, “Do it a third time,” and they did it a third time.
The water ran around the altar, and they filled the trench with water.

At the time for offering the sacrifice, Elijah cried out to heaven and said, “Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let them know today that you are the Lord, the God of Israel, and that I am your servant and have done these things.
“Hear me, Lord; answer me with fire, so that this people may know that you are the Lord God and that you have turned the heart of this people back.”
Fire fell from the Lord out of heaven and consumed the burnt offerings, the wood, and the earth, and the fire devoured the water in the trench.
When all the people saw this, they fell on their faces and said, “Truly, the Lord is God! The Lord is God!”
Elijah said to the people, “Seize the prophets of Baal, and let none of them escape.” They seized them, and Elijah brought them down to the Kishon ravine and slaughtered them there.
And Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of approaching rain.”
Ahab went up to eat and drink, and Elijah went up to the summit of Mount Carmel. He bowed down to the ground and put his face between his knees.
He said to his young servant, “Go up and look toward the sea.” The young servant went up, looked, and said, “There is nothing.” Elijah said, “Please go back seven times.”

The young servant went back seven times. After the seventh time, there was a small cloud like a man’s hand drawing up water. Elijah said, “Go up and tell Ahab, ‘Harness your chariot and go down, lest the rain overtake you.’”
While he was going back and forth, the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and there was heavy rain. Ahab was weeping as he traveled to Jezreel.
The hand of the Lord came upon Elijah. He tightened his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to the entrance of Jezreel.
Ahab told his wife Jezebel everything Elijah had done and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.

Jezebel sent messengers to Elijah, saying, “If you are Elijah, I am Jezebel! May the gods do this to me and more besides if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them.”
Elijah was afraid, got up, and went away alone. He came to Beersheba in the land of Judah and left his young servant there.

And he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness. He went and sat beneath a terebinth tree and asked that he might die, saying, “It is enough now, Lord. Take my life from me, Lord, for I am no better than my fathers.”
He fell asleep and slept under the shrub. Then someone approached him and said, “Get up and eat.”
And Elijah looked, and there at his head were a cake of spelt and a jug of water. He got up, ate and drank, and lay down to sleep again.
And the angel of the Lord approached him a second time and said to him, “Get up and eat, for the journey ahead is too much for you.”
And he got up, ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, until he reached the mountain of God at Horeb.
And he entered the cave there and stayed. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him and said, “Why are you here, Elijah?”

And Elijah said, “I have been intensely zealous for the Lord Almighty, because the Israelites have abandoned you, demolished your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and they seek to take my life.”

And he said, “Go out tomorrow and stand on the mountain there before the Lord. And behold, the Lord will pass by.” And a great, powerful wind tore apart the mountains and shattered the rocks before the Lord, but the Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind came an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.
And after the earthquake came fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire came the sound of a gentle breeze.
And when Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his sheepskin cloak, went out, and stood beneath the cave. And behold, a voice came to him and said, “Why are you here, Elijah?”

And Elijah said, “I have been intensely zealous for the Lord Almighty, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant, torn down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I alone am left, and they seek to take my life.”
And the Lord said to him, “Go and retrace your way, and take the road through the wilderness of Damascus. Go and anoint Hazael as king of the Syrians,
and Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel; and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah, as prophet in your place.
And Jehu will kill whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, and Elisha will kill whoever escapes the sword of Jehu.
And you shall leave seven thousand men in Israel: all whose knees have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him.”

And he went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve oxen, with pairs of oxen before him, and he himself was with the twelve. And Elijah came up to him and threw his sheepskin cloak over him.
And Elisha left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, “Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” And he said to him, “Go back, for what have I done to you?”

And he turned back from him, took the pairs of oxen, and slaughtered them. He cooked them using the oxen’s equipment, and gave the meat to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah, and served him.

And Ben-hadad, king of the Syrians, gathered all his forces, went up, and besieged Samaria. Thirty-two kings were with him, and all the horses and chariots went up and besieged Samaria and fought against it.
And he sent messengers into the city to Ahab, king of Israel,
and said to him, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘Your silver and your gold are mine, and your wives and your handsome sons are mine.’”
The king of Israel answered and said, “As you have said, my lord the king, I and everything I have are yours.”
And the messengers returned and said, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘I sent word that you should give me your silver, your gold, your wives, and your sons.
For tomorrow at this time I will send my servants, and they will search your house and the houses of your servants. Whatever is desirable in their eyes, they will lay their hands on it and take it.’”

And the king of Israel called together all the elders of the land and said, “Understand and see that he is seeking trouble, for he sent to me concerning my sons and my daughters, my silver and my gold, and I did not withhold them from him.”
And the elders and all the people said to him, “Do not listen and do not agree.”

He said to Ben-hadad’s messengers, “Tell your lord the king: ‘I will do everything you sent word to your servant about the first time, but I cannot do this thing.’” The men went and brought him the answer.
Ben-hadad sent word to him and said, “May the gods do such and such to me, and more besides, if the dust of Samaria, together with its bricks, is enough for all the foot soldiers of my army!”
The king of Israel answered, “Enough now! Let the bent man not boast as though he were upright.”
When this answer was given to him, he was drinking wine with all the kings who were with him in the tents. He said to his servants, “Build a siege ramp.” And they set up a siege ramp around the city.

Then a prophet approached Ahab king of Israel and said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Do you see that great multitude? Look, I will hand them over to you today, and you will know that I am the Lord.’”
Ahab said, “By whom?” He answered, “This is what the Lord says: ‘By the young servants of the provincial governors.’” Ahab said, “Who will begin the battle?” He answered, “You.”
He mustered the servants of the provincial governors, and there were two hundred and thirty. Then he mustered all the people, all the fighting men—seven thousand men—and went out at noon.
Ben-hadad was drinking wine and was drunk at Succoth, along with the thirty-two kings who were his allies.
The young servants of the provincial governors went out first. They sent word to Ben-hadad and reported to him, saying, “Men have come out of Samaria.”
He said to them, “If they have come out for peace, take them alive; and if they have come out for battle, take them alive.”
The young servants of the provincial governors came out of the city, with the army following them.
Each man struck down the man he encountered. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them. Ben-hadad king of the Syrians escaped on horseback with some three horsemen.
The king of Israel went out and captured the horses and chariots, and inflicted very heavy losses on the Syrians.

The prophet approached the king of Israel and said to him, “Strengthen yourself, and consider carefully what you must do, for at the turn of this year Ben-hadad king of the Syrians will come against you.”

The servants of the king of the Syrians said to him, “The God of Israel is a god of the mountains and not a god of the plains. That is why they defeated us. If we fight them on level ground, we will defeat them.”
“Do this: remove the kings from their respective positions and appoint commanders in their place.”
“We will replace your army with an army like the one you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. We will fight them on level ground and defeat them.” He listened to them and did so.
At the turn of the year, Ben-hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel.
The Israelites mustered, divided into two companies, and advanced to meet them. The Israelites drew up against the Syrians like two herds of goats, while the Syrians filled the land.

The man of God approached the king of Israel and said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘Because the Syrians said that the Lord, the God of Israel, is a god of the mountains and not a god of the plains, he will hand that great army over to you, and you will know that I am the Lord.’”
They camped opposite one another for seven days. On the seventh day the battle began, and Israel struck down one hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in a single day.
The survivors fled to Aphek, their city, and the wall fell on the twenty-seven thousand men who remained. Ben-hadad fled and entered his house, going from room to room.

His servants said to him, “Look, we know that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Let us put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads, and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare our lives.”
They put sackcloth around their waists and ropes on their heads, and said to the king of Israel, “Your servant Ben-hadad says, ‘Let me live.’” He said, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.”

The men took this as an omen and [?], and caught the words from his mouth. They said, “Your brother Ben-hadad is here.” He said, “Go in and bring him.” Ben-hadad came out to him, and they brought him up into the chariot with him.

He said to him, “I will return to you the cities that my father took from your father, and you shall levy tribute for yourself in Damascus, as my father imposed it in Samaria.” He said, “And I will release you under a covenant.” He made a covenant with him and released him.
And a man from among the sons of the prophets said to his companion, by the word of the Lord, “Strike me.” But the man would not strike him.
He said to him, “Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord, a lion will kill you as soon as you leave me.” When he left him, a lion found him and killed him.
He found another man and said, “Strike me.” The man struck him, striking and injuring him severely.
The prophet went and stood before the king on the road, and bound a cloth over his eyes.

As the king passed that way, he cried out to the king and said, “Your servant went out with the army into battle, and a man brought another man to me and said, ‘Guard this man. If he escapes, your life shall be in place of his life, or you shall weigh out a talent of silver.’
“While your servant was looking here and there, the man was nowhere to be found.” The king of Israel said to him, “Look, that too is a trap on my part. Did you kill him, then?”
He quickly removed the cloth from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets.
He said to him, “Thus says the Lord: Because you let the harmful man escape from my hands, your life shall be in place of his life, and your people in place of his people.”
The king of Israel went home sorrowful and dejected, and came to Samaria.
After these things, there was a vineyard belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite near the threshing floor of Ahab, king of Samaria.

The king spoke to Naboth and said, “Give me your vineyard, so that I may have it as a vegetable garden, because it is near my house. I will give you another vineyard better than it. Or, if it pleases you, I will give you silver as the price of your vineyard, and it shall be a vegetable garden for me.”
Naboth said to the king, “May my God forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my ancestors.”

Ahab came home sorrowful and dejected because of the words Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him, saying, “I will not give you the inheritance of my ancestors.” He lay down on his bed, covered his face, and ate no food.
His wife Jezebel came in to him, spoke with him, and said, “Why is your spirit troubled, and why are you not eating?”

He said to her, “Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said, ‘Give me your vineyard for silver, or, if you wish, I will give you another vineyard in its place.’ But he said, ‘I will not give you the inheritance of my ancestors.’”
And his wife Jezebel said to him, “Is this how you exercise kingship over Israel? Get up, eat some bread, and regain your composure. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
She wrote a letter in Ahab’s name, sealed it with his ring, and sent the letter to the elders and nobles of his city who lived with Naboth.
The letter was written as follows: “Observe a fast, and seat Naboth at the head of the people.”
And seat two lawless men opposite him, and let them testify against him and say, ‘You cursed God and the king.’ Then take him out and stone him to death.
And the men of his city, the elders and nobles who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had instructed them, just as it was written in the letters.
They proclaimed a fast and seated Naboth at the head of the people.

And two lawless men came and sat opposite him. These rebellious men testified against Naboth before all the people, saying, ‘Naboth cursed God and the king.’ They took him outside the city and stoned him with stones, and he died.
And they sent word to Jezebel, saying, ‘Naboth has been stoned and is dead.’

When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, ‘Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to sell you for silver, for Naboth is no longer alive; he is dead.’
When Ahab heard that Naboth the Jezreelite was dead, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth. After this, Ahab got up and went down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite to take possession of it.
And the Lord spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, saying:
‘Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria, for he has gone down to Naboth’s vineyard to take possession of it.

Speak to him and say, “This is what the Lord says: Since you have killed and taken possession, therefore this is what the Lord says: In the place where dogs and pigs licked up Naboth’s blood, they will lick up your blood, and prostitutes will wash themselves in your blood.”’
And Ahab said to Elijah, ‘Have you found me, my enemy?’ He said, ‘I have found you, because you have vainly exalted yourself to do evil before the Lord and provoke him to anger.
Look, I will bring disaster upon you and burn up those who come after you. I will wipe out from Ahab’s household everyone who urinates against a wall, both the oppressed and the abandoned in Israel.
I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because of the provocations with which you angered me and caused Israel to sin.’
And concerning Jezebel the Lord spoke, saying, ‘Dogs will eat her by the wall of Jezreel.’
‘Dogs will eat anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city, and the birds of the sky will eat anyone belonging to him who dies in the open country.’
Yet Ahab vainly exalted himself to do evil before the Lord, as Jezebel his wife led him astray.
And he acted most abominably by following abominable idols, according to everything the Amorites had done, whom the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.

Because of this word, the king humbled himself before the Lord. He went about weeping, tore his robe, put sackcloth on his body, and fasted. He put on sackcloth on the day when he killed Naboth the Jezreelite, and went about bent over.
And the word of the Lord came through his servant Elijah concerning Ahab, and the Lord said:
‘Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has bowed down before me, I will not bring disaster in his days, but in his son’s days I will bring disaster upon his house.’
And they remained at peace for three years, and there was no war between the Syrians and Israel.
In the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to the king of Israel.
And the king of Israel said to his servants, ‘Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us? Yet we remain silent instead of taking it from the hands of the king of Syria.’

And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, ‘Will you go with us to battle at Ramoth-gilead?’ Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, ‘I am as you are, my troops are as your troops, and my horses are as your horses.’
And Jehoshaphat king of Judah said to the king of Israel, ‘Please inquire of the Lord today.’

The king of Israel gathered all the prophets, about four hundred men, and the king said to them, “Shall I go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I stay here?” They said, “Go up, and the Lord will surely deliver it into the king’s hands.”
And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Is there perhaps a prophet of the Lord here or not, so that we may inquire of the Lord through him?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is one man here through whom we can inquire of the Lord, but I hate him because he speaks nothing good about me, only evil: Micaiah son of Imlah.” Jehoshaphat king of Judah said, “The king should not speak that way.”
The king of Israel called a eunuch and said, “Quickly bring Micaiah son of Imlah here.”
The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting, each on his own throne, wearing armor at the gates of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.
And Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made himself iron horns and said, “This is what the Lord says: With these you will gore the Syrians until they are wiped out.”
All the prophets were prophesying the same thing, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and succeed, and the Lord will deliver the king of Syria into your hands.”
The messenger who went to summon Micaiah told him, “Look, all the prophets speak good things about the king with one voice. Now let your word be like that of one of them, and speak good things.”
Micaiah said, “As the Lord lives, I will speak only what the Lord tells me.”

He came to the king, and the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall I go up to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I stay here?” He said, “Go up and succeed, and the Lord will deliver it into the king’s hands.”
The king said to him, “Again, for a second time, I have put you under oath to speak truthfully to me in the name of the Lord.”
He said, “It is not so. I saw all Israel scattered over the mountains like a flock that has no shepherd. The Lord said, ‘These have no masters. Let each return to his own home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Did I not tell you that he prophesies nothing good for me, only evil?”

And Micaiah said, “Not so—not I. But hear the message of the Lord. Did I not indeed see the Lord, the God of Israel, seated on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing around him, on his right and on his left?”
The Lord said, “Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, so that he will go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” One said one thing, and another said another.
A spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, “I will deceive him.”
The Lord said to him, “How?” He said, “I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.” He said, “You will deceive him and succeed. Go out and do so.”
“And now, look, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the Lord has spoken of disaster against you.”
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached and struck Micaiah on the jaw, saying, “Which Spirit of the Lord was it that passed from me and spoke through you?”
Micaiah said, “You yourself will see on that day when you go from room to room to hide.”
The king of Israel said, “Seize Micaiah and hand him over to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king’s son.
“And say, ‘This is what the king says: Put this man in prison, and let him have the bread of hardship and the water of hardship until I return in peace.’”
Micaiah said, “If you do indeed return in peace, then the Lord has not spoken through me.” And he said, “Listen, all you troops!”
The king of Israel went up to Ramoth-gilead, and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went with him.
And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “I will disguise myself and go into battle, and you put on my clothes.” And the king of Israel disguised himself and entered the battle.
The king of Syria gave his chariot commanders this order: “Do not fight anyone, great or small, but only the king of Israel.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat king of Judah, they said to one another, “It seems that this is the king of Israel.” They surrounded him to fight, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned away from him.

A man drew his bow with strength and struck the king of Israel between the armor and the breastplate. The king said to his chariot driver, “Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am wounded.”

The battle grew fiercer that day, and the king stood on his chariot facing the Syrians from morning until evening. Blood flowed from his wound and filled the bottom of the chariot, and toward evening he died.
At sunset a herald stood in the army’s camp and said, “Everyone to his own city and his own land, for the king is dead!”
He came to Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.
They washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria, and pigs and dogs licked up his blood, and prostitutes bathed in the blood, according to the word that the Lord had spoken.
The rest of the acts of Ahab, everything he did, the ivory house he built, and all the cities he built—these are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Ahab rested with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king in his place.
And Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah; he became king in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother’s name was Azubah, daughter of Shilhi.
He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn aside from them, doing what was right before the Lord.
Except that he did not remove the high places, for the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places.
Jehoshaphat was at peace with the king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, the mighty deeds he performed, and all his warfare—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
He removed from the land the remaining shrine prostitutes who had remained in the days of his father.
There was no established king in Edom.
King Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they did not go, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let your servants go with my servants, and your ships with my ships.” But Jehoshaphat was unwilling.
Jehoshaphat rested with his ancestors and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David his ancestor, and his son Jehoram became king in his place.
Ahaziah son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel for two years.
He did evil before the Lord and followed the ways of his father Ahab and the ways of his mother Jezebel, and the sins of the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin.
And he served the Baals and bowed down to them, and provoked the Lord, the God of Israel, to anger, just as all those before him had done.
